rotate_img — 2D geometry op

• Data kinds: image → image

• Call: fullseye.apply(img, "rotate_img", a=0.5, b=0.5) (the 2-D model is one image plus two scalar knobs a,b∈[0,1])

• HALCON equivalent: rotate_image (the HALCON reference is a useful guide to its meaning and parameters)

*The figure is the actual output on a synthetic 128×128 input. Left: input, right: output. Point clouds are drawn as a top-down scatter (brightness = z), 1-D series as a line plot, volumes as the maximum-intensity projection along z, videos as the middle frame, complex images as magnitude; return values that are not pictures are shown as the values themselves.*

Sweeping knob a (0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9, the other knob at its default):

▸ rotate_img: knob a sweep (docs site)

*Knob b does not change the output (measured: identical at 0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9).*

On other images (synthetic scene / photo / coins. Top row: inputs, bottom row: their outputs. Knobs at default):

▸ rotate_img: other inputs (docs site)

*The 4th column is a colour (H,W,3) input. This op handles colour without crossing channels (it does not convolve the colour channel as a third spatial axis).*

Usage

Rotate about the image centre by -45° + 90°·a (a=0.5 → 0°). b unused.

★Calling convention (documented on 2026-09-02; the implementation was not changed):

• The canvas is not changed (reshape=False). The output shape is the same as the input, and pixels that leave the frame through rotation are discarded.

• Outside the frame is filled by mirroring (mode="reflect"). So rotating makes the original image fold back and appear in the four corners (rotating a form makes mirrored characters appear in the corners).

Which is canonical depends on the use. The canon of this op is "chaining it always yields an image of the same shape and the same value range" — the evolution pipeline connects images between stages unconditionally, so if the shape changes or a constant enters outside the frame, downstream statistics (mean, variance, histogram) move depending on the rotation amount. Mirroring keeps the image's own statistics rather than "a constant made from nothing", so for this use it is the one adopted.

Not suitable for deskew (correcting the tilt of a form): the folded-back mirrored characters ride along into OCR / binarisation as they are. If you want to fill with the background colour, do not use this op; call scipy.ndimage.rotate(v, ang, reshape=True, mode="constant", cval=bg) directly (the 2-knob interface of fullseye.apply cannot pass a background colour). The same convention applies as is to rotate_image in backends_auto (_sh_geom kind="rotate") as well.
